title: All the Gold In Fort Knox: Meh
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Fort Knox, from its origins as a U.S. Army training camp (Camp Knox, named for Henry Knox) to its use as the United States Bullion Depository for the nation's gold. They cover how the gold was moved from New York and Philadelphia in 1937-1938 with decoy trains, the vault's security features (multi-person combination, time-delay lock, two-foot granite and steel walls, minefield, escape tunnel, mirrors), the gold bar weights and the statutory value of gold at $42.22 per ounce, and a rough calculation of the gold's worth. They discuss rare coins and documents stored there (Declaration of Independence, Bill of Rights, Gettysburg Address, Gutenberg Bible, Magna Carta), the conspiracy theories claiming the gold is gone (including Peter Beter, Ron Paul, and anti-Semitic Rothschild theories), and the history of the gold standard, its end under Roosevelt and Nixon, and why the gold is still kept. The episode closes with listener mail about cattails.
topics: Declaration of Independence Fort Knox storage

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about listener feedback about Chuck disagreeing, then introduce the episode on Fort Knox and the United States Bullion Depository.

segments.title: History of Fort Knox and moving the gold
segments.summary: Camp Knox began as an Army training camp in 1903 in West Point, Kentucky, was made permanent in 1918, and became Fort Knox in 1932. In the 1930s the Mint took part of it for the gold bullion depository, built in 1937-1938 at about half a million dollars. Gold was moved from New York and Philadelphia, partly to protect it from coastal invasion, with decoy trains and guards. Silver went to Denver.
topics: gold transfer from New York and Philadelphia

segments.title: Tours of Fort Knox
segments.summary: Fort Knox is essentially closed to tours. Only three official tours are known: one by FDR, one congressional delegation in the 1970s, and one in 2017 led by Steven Mnuchin.

segments.title: Vault security and building design
segments.summary: The vault requires multiple people with partial combinations and has a time-delay lock of about four days. The vault sits inside a building surrounded by a wide field said to be a minefield, with granite and steel walls, fabricated steel walls, mirrors for surveillance, machine gun turrets, a blast, drill and torch proof door, an escape tunnel that opens only from inside, an on-site gun range, and independent water and power.

segments.title: Gold bars, weight, and value
segments.summary: Each gold bar weighs about 27.5 pounds (400 troy ounces). The hosts estimate Fort Knox holds about 40 metric tons of gold, roughly 2.5 percent of all gold ever mined, and compute a value of about $6.2 to $6.8 billion using the statutory value of $42.22 per ounce.

segments.title: Other items stored at Fort Knox
segments.summary: Fort Knox holds rare coins not released to the public, including a 1933 double eagle and an aluminum penny, and has stored documents such as the Declaration of Independence, Bill of Rights, Gettysburg Address, Gutenberg Bible, and the Magna Carta during World War II. The documents were returned after the war.

segments.title: Gold conspiracy theories
segments.summary: The hosts discuss popular claims that the gold is missing or fake, including claims by Peter Beter, Ron Paul, the Rothschild family, and Kustaa Jansen (Yan Nieven Huis). They note many of these theories are anti-Semitic and that some economists and officials, including Alan Greenspan and Judy Shelton, have supported returning to the gold standard.

segments.title: Gold standard, paper money, and why gold is still kept
segments.summary: The hosts explain why paper currency was backed by gold and how the gold standard was limited, with the Federal Reserve established in 1913, Roosevelt weakening the link in the 1930s, and Nixon ending convertibility in 1971. They explain why Fort Knox still holds gold: national pride and avoiding disruption to the gold market.
topics: why the US still holds gold
